stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the hospital after a day of high-grade fever, progressive headaches, and double vision.  The patient has experienced purulent nasal drainage and frontal headaches for the past several days.  He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus.  Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 94/min.  Physical examination shows ptosis, mydriasis, mild proptosis, and loss of the corneal reflex of the right eye.  Visual acuity is normal in both eyes, but the patient is unable to move the right eye in any direction.  There is decreased sensation in the right upper face.  Which of the following structures is most likely involved in this patient's presentation?​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌
explanation:
This patient with signs of a sinus infection (eg, fever, purulent nasal drainage) now has multiple cranial nerve abnormalities, findings concerning for the development of septic cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST).  The formation of a clot in the cavernous sinus is most often due to the retrograde spread of infection through the valveless facial venous system from the orbits, sinuses (ethmoidal or sphenoidal), or teeth.

Patients with CST typically experience headaches and fever.  Proptosis (eye protrusion) and chemosis (conjunctival swelling) may also be evident due to impaired venous drainage through the ophthalmic veins.  CST can present with varying unilateral or bilateral cranial nerve abnormalities, often including the following:

  • Ptosis and miosis:  oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  • Partial or complete ocular muscle paralysis:  CN III, trochlear nerve (CN IV), and abducens nerve (CN VI)
  • Reduced sensation in the upper two-thirds of the face:  ophthalmic (CN V1) and maxillary (CN V2) portions of the trigeminal nerve
  • Impaired corneal reflex:  CN V1 afferent limb

Common pathogens that precipitate CST include Staphylococcus aureus (most common) and streptococci; fungal organisms (eg, Mucor, Rhizopus) are also possible.

(Choice A)  Although the cranial nerves exit through the brainstem, they do so from different portions (eg, optic nerve [CN II] and CN IV from the midbrain, CN V and CN VI from the pons).  A lesion involving all of these nerves would be extensive and result in other neurologic signs such as contralateral hemiparesis, vertigo, and ataxia.

(Choice C)  Frontal lobe pathology can cause disinhibition, difficulty planning/organizing, and personality changes.  Cranial nerve deficits are not characteristic.

(Choice D)  The inferior orbital fissure transmits branches of the maxillary division of CN V, infraorbital vessels, and branches from the sphenopalatine ganglion; no nerves to the eye muscles pass through this fissure.

(Choice E)  Lesions of the jugular foramen can result in jugular foramen syndrome, which is characterized by the dysfunction of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus nerve (CN X), and accessory nerve (CN XI).  Findings include dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of gag reflex on the ipsilateral side, and deviation of the uvula toward the contralateral side.

(Choice F)  The optic chiasm is superior to the cavernous sinus, where the optic nerve (CN II) fibers from the nasal side of each retina cross to the opposite side of the brain.  Optic chiasm lesions typically cause bitemporal hemianopia.

Educational objective:Infection of the orbits, sinuses, or teeth may spread through the valveless facial venous system into the cavernous sinus, resulting in cavernous sinus thrombosis.  Patients typically have headaches, fever, and deficits in the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and trigeminal nerve (CN V, ophthalmic and maxillary branches).​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌
